div.p: Only after fsync returns is the write durable. With interval, you may lose up to that window on power loss — that is a documented product decision, not an accident. Redis ships the same tradeoff.

Crash after step 4, before step 6 → the record is on disk. Replay re-applies it. The client never got an ack, so a retry is idempotent: PUT is an upsert, and re-applying a vector the graph already holds changes nothing.
Crash before step 4 completes → torn tail record. CRC fails on recovery, the log truncates there, the write simply never happened. Both outcomes are consistent.
registry lookup; create or load the collection if cold
monotonic LSN — orders the WAL and marks where a snapshot ends

g.text: 5a · Is this id already live? — the upsert branch

p.strong: Why not just overwrite node.vector in place?

div.p: The slot's index is referenced by neighbor lists all over the graph, and those edges were chosen for the OLD vector — they claim "these two are close" about a pair that no longer is. Searches would keep being routed in from a region the vector has left.

Repairing them is not available either: pruning makes edges asymmetric, so a node's own neighbor list is not the list of nodes pointing at it. Finding every inbound edge means scanning the whole graph, O(N·M) per update.
A fresh slot is correct by construction. It costs one dead slot — the same debt Delete takes on, paid to the same compaction pass.
always — safe, ~1–10 ms/write on consumer NVMe interval — group commit, default ~50 ms never — tests and benchmarks only
Copies so the graph never aliases a caller buffer. Normalizes for Cosine, collapsing it to 1 - dot(a,b).

ids[id] hit, new vector → tombstone the old slot

A replacement draws a fresh level; it does not inherit the height of the slot it replaced.

ol.li: seed next layer with the closest hit

div.p: slices.Equal against the stored form. No tombstone, no slot, no edge touched.

This is the WAL-replay path: recovery re-applies records the graph already holds, and if that cost a slot every restart would inflate the graph with tombstones for vectors that never changed. 332 ns, against 776 µs for a real replacement.

ol.li: node.deleted = true — the slot stays, keeping its index and every edge it has
was this slot the entry? → reelectEntry(), or the descent below starts from a corpse

div.p: Inside Insert's own write lock, never by calling Delete — that would open a window where the id belongs to nobody, and a reader would observe an update as a disappearance.
